skill: Adapting the planning lifecycle to a multi-site rollout program rather than a single, discrete project
scenario: A telecom operator has contracted a rollout of 500 new 5G small-cell sites across a metropolitan area over 18 months. Each site follows a broadly similar sequence (site acquisition, permitting, civil works, equipment install, RF commissioning) but sites start on a rolling basis as permits are secured, and the number of active sites at any time can range from a handful to over 80.
question: Describe how the planning lifecycle and schedule structure for this kind of high-volume rollout program should differ from a single discrete construction project, and what would go wrong if a planner simply applied a single-project mindset.
expectedAnswer: A rollout program of this kind needs a template-driven, repeatable planning approach rather than a bespoke schedule per site: a standard site-level activity template (with typical durations and logic) is developed once, validated, and then instantiated per site as permits are secured, with site-specific dates and any local variations layered on top. The lifecycle becomes continuous and rolling rather than a single linear baseline-to-close-out arc — new sites are constantly entering the pipeline while others are completing, so schedule structure must support portfolio-level reporting (how many sites are in each phase, overall program completion rate/velocity) alongside individual site tracking. A single-project mindset (building 500 individually bespoke, hand-crafted schedules, or trying to force all 500 sites into one gigantic simultaneously-baselined network) would be unmanageable to update, would not reflect the true rolling-start nature of the work, and would make portfolio-level throughput trends (are we completing sites faster or slower than planned, on average) very hard to see.
strongAnswer: Describes using a template/typical-activity-set (sometimes called a 'template project' or standard fragnet in P6) that is copied or linked per site, combined with an EPS/WBS structure organized by site with portfolio-level rollup, and metrics focused on rate of throughput (sites entering/completing each phase per month) rather than only individual critical path analysis per site.
expertAnswer: Notes that the real planning challenge in a rollout program is less about CPM logic per site (which is usually simple and repetitive) and more about capacity/resource-constrained scheduling across sites — permitting throughput, crew availability, and equipment lead time are usually the actual bottleneck, so the planning approach should incorporate resource leveling and pipeline/queue management across the portfolio, and the reporting cadence should track program velocity and forecast completion trend (e.g., sites/month) the way a production-line or manufacturing operation would, rather than treating each site as an independent one-off critical path exercise.
explanation: High-volume, repeatable-scope rollout programs require a fundamentally different planning lifecycle than a single bespoke project: template standardization, rolling/continuous baselining as sites enter the pipeline, and portfolio-level throughput reporting replace the single linear plan-baseline-execute-close arc.
reasoning: When scope repeats hundreds of times with a rolling start, the dominant planning challenge shifts from per-site CPM complexity (which is usually low) to standardization, resource/capacity constraints across many concurrent sites, and portfolio-level visibility — a single-project approach does not scale to that volume and misses the real driver of overall program pace.
commonMistakes: Proposing to build 500 fully bespoke schedules instead of a standardized, reusable template.
Focusing only on individual site critical paths and ignoring resource/capacity constraints across the portfolio.
Not addressing how new sites enter the schedule on a rolling basis rather than all starting together.
redFlags: Cannot describe any mechanism for standardizing repeated scope across sites.
Has no concept of portfolio-level throughput or velocity reporting distinct from single-project percent complete.

skill: Choosing a resource/production-rate-driven schedule development approach for linear, repetitive underground works over a purely activity-logic approach
scenario: A mining contractor is developing the schedule for sinking and equipping a 900-meter deep vertical shaft. The work is essentially a single, continuous, repetitive cycle (drill, blast, muck out, support/lining) advancing a few meters per cycle, day after day, with a single crew and a single set of shaft-bottom equipment — there is very little parallel work possible.
question: Would you develop this schedule primarily as a traditional activity-by-activity CPM network, or take a different approach? Explain your reasoning and describe what you would actually build.
expectedAnswer: For this kind of single-resource, repetitive-cycle, effectively linear operation, a traditional CPM network broken into hundreds of individually logic-linked 'advance meter X to X+3' activities adds complexity without adding real analytical value, because there is almost no parallelism to model — the true schedule driver is simply the achievable production/advance rate (meters per day or per week) applied to the total depth, similar to a linear/repetitive scheduling method used for tunnels, pipelines, or highways. The appropriate approach is to develop the shaft-sinking duration primarily from a production-rate calculation (validated advance rate per cycle, based on ground conditions, blast/muck cycle time, and any known variable zones such as water-bearing strata), representing it in the schedule as either a small number of representative CPM activities per major depth zone or as a resource-loaded linear/velocity model, rather than an artificially detailed CPM breakdown of every few meters. CPM logic remains useful at the interfaces — start-up, equipping, commissioning of shaft services — where real parallel work and dependencies exist.
strongAnswer: Explicitly names this as a linear/repetitive scheduling situation and distinguishes it from typical multi-trade building work where CPM's strength (modeling many parallel, interdependent paths) is actually needed; notes the production rate itself should be substantiated with real data (comparable shaft-sinking rates, ground investigation results) rather than an assumed round number, since the entire schedule's credibility rests on that single rate.
expertAnswer: Flags the risk-management implication: because there is only one resource/crew and no parallel path to fall back on, any single delay to the advance rate (equipment breakdown, unexpected ground conditions, water ingress) translates almost directly into schedule delay with no logic-network absorption capacity elsewhere — so the schedule risk analysis for this kind of project should focus heavily on production-rate variability and contingency for the recognized zones of geotechnical uncertainty, rather than on CPM float management, which has limited relevance when the entire critical path is effectively one continuous resource-constrained operation.
explanation: CPM's core strength — resolving many parallel interdependent paths into one calculated critical path — has little to add when there is fundamentally only one path and one constrained resource; in that situation, a production-rate/linear scheduling approach communicates the real schedule driver more transparently than an artificially granular activity network would.
reasoning: Schedule development approach should match the actual nature of the work: highly parallel, multi-trade scope benefits from detailed CPM logic; single-resource, repetitive, linear-progress scope (shaft sinking, tunneling, highway paving, pipeline laying) is better represented by production-rate-driven duration calculation, because CPM's parallel-path analytical power is simply not being used and excessive activity-level granularity there adds administrative burden without adding insight.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to a highly granular activity-by-activity CPM breakdown regardless of whether the work is actually parallel or purely sequential/linear.
Treating production rate as a simple assumed number rather than something that must be substantiated by data.
Not recognizing that risk analysis focus should shift from float/logic-network risk to production-rate variability risk for this kind of work.
redFlags: Insists on building hundreds of near-identical CPM activities for a purely linear operation with no analytical justification.
Cannot explain what a production-rate/linear scheduling approach is or when it is appropriate.

followUpQuestions.prompt: How would you build contingency into this schedule for a recognized zone of poor or water-bearing ground at, say, 400-450 meters depth?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate can translate the production-rate approach into a concrete risk-adjusted schedule.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Once the shaft reaches the bottom and multiple parallel equipping/outfitting trades mobilize, does the same production-rate approach still apply?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate recognizes the approach should switch back to CPM logic once real parallelism exists.

skill: Correctly stating the behavior of a Start-to-Start relationship with a positive lag
scenario: In a cold storage warehouse construction schedule, 'Install Wall Insulated Panels' and 'Install Roof Insulated Panels' are linked with a Start-to-Start (SS) relationship carrying a 4-working-day lag, reflecting that the roof crew can begin once the wall crew is four days into their run and has cleared enough of the building perimeter for crane access.
question: True or False: With this Start-to-Start relationship and 4-day lag, 'Install Roof Insulated Panels' cannot start until 'Install Wall Insulated Panels' has been underway for at least 4 working days, but it does not need to wait for wall panel installation to finish.

options.label: True
options.text: True

options.label: False
options.text: False

explanation: A Start-to-Start relationship ties the successor's start to the predecessor's start, not its finish. With a 4-day lag, the roof panel installation's earliest start is 4 working days after the wall panel installation's start — it can then run in parallel with the remaining wall panel work, reflecting real overlapping trade execution, which is exactly the kind of relationship type suited to two crews progressively working the same building from different faces.
reasoning: SS relationships are the correct modeling choice whenever a successor can genuinely begin before its predecessor finishes, once a defined portion of the predecessor's work or a physical condition (here, crane access after some wall progress) has been achieved — the lag quantifies how much of that head start is required.
commonMistakes: Confusing SS with FS and assuming the roof work must wait for all wall panels to be installed first.
Assuming a lag on an SS relationship must mean the same thing as a lag on an FS relationship.
redFlags: Cannot distinguish how a lag applies differently depending on the relationship type it is attached to.
p6Checks: Activities view — Relationships tab to confirm relationship type is SS (not FS) and the lag value and units (working vs calendar days) are correct.

skill: Distinguishing a recovery schedule from a re-baselined schedule and from the original baseline
scenario: A shopping mall redevelopment project has fallen 35 working days behind its approved baseline. The client asks the contractor to submit a 'recovery schedule' showing how the lost time will be won back without extending the contract completion date.
question: What is the correct understanding of a recovery schedule in this context?

options.label: A
options.text: A recovery schedule proposes a revised execution plan — such as added resources, resequencing, extended working hours, or overlapping activities — intended to regain lost time against the original contract completion date; it is a plan of intended corrective action, not a new baseline that resets the target date

options.label: B
options.text: A recovery schedule automatically becomes the new baseline the moment it is submitted, replacing the original approved baseline

options.label: C
options.text: A recovery schedule is simply the current schedule renamed, with no changes to logic, resources, or durations

options.label: D
options.text: A recovery schedule is only ever prepared by the client, never by the contractor

explanation: A recovery schedule is a specific, targeted execution plan showing how the contractor intends to regain lost time and still meet (or come as close as possible to) the original contract completion date — through concrete, resourced measures, not just wishful compression of durations. It does not automatically become the new baseline (B); the original baseline typically remains the reference for variance and any entitlement analysis unless and until a re-baseline is formally agreed and approved through change control. It requires real changes to the plan, not a relabeling exercise (C), and is normally contractor-prepared and client-reviewed/accepted, not client-authored (D).
reasoning: Recovery schedules, re-baselines, and the original baseline serve different purposes and should not be conflated: the original baseline remains the fixed reference for measuring overall variance and supporting any entitlement position; a recovery schedule is a forward-looking corrective action plan measured against that same original target; and a re-baseline is a formal, approved reset of the reference itself, typically reserved for cases where the original baseline is no longer achievable or relevant (e.g., after an agreed extension of time).
commonMistakes: Assuming submitting a recovery schedule silently resets the baseline.
Treating 'recovery schedule' as just a cosmetic renaming with no real plan changes behind it.
Not recognizing that acceptance of a recovery schedule by the client does not, by itself, constitute an agreed extension of time or a waiver of the contractor's obligation to meet the original date.
redFlags: Cannot distinguish a recovery schedule from a re-baseline.
Believes a recovery schedule changes contractual completion obligations automatically.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If the recovery schedule's proposed measures (e.g., double shifts) carry real cost, who typically bears that cost, and does that depend on the cause of the original delay?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests awareness that recovery cost allocation is a contractual/causation question, not a scheduling one.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What would make you recommend a re-baseline instead of a recovery schedule in a similar situation?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests judgment on when recovery is realistic versus when the original date is no longer achievable at all.

skill: Recognizing that a technically correct CPM update can still misrepresent reality when the underlying methodology was never validated against actual site conditions
scenario: On a university campus student housing building, the planning engineer updates the schedule every week strictly by collecting percent-complete figures from foremen and entering them into P6, recalculating the network, and issuing the updated report. He has not visited the site or spoken with the site engineer about actual construction sequencing in over two months, relying entirely on the numbers he is given.
question: Is this engineer performing planning, scheduling, or both? What risk does his approach create?
expectedAnswer: He is performing scheduling (mechanically processing status inputs through the CPM engine) but not planning (validating that the logic, sequence and reported progress still reflect real, achievable site conditions). The risk is that the schedule can silently drift away from reality: foremen's self-reported percent-complete figures may be optimistic, inconsistent, or based on different definitions of 'complete' across trades, and without periodic site validation the planning engineer has no way to catch outdated logic (sequences that no longer reflect how the work is actually being executed), overstated progress, or emerging site issues before they show up as a hard slip in the numbers.
strongAnswer: Recommends a concrete practice: periodic site walks (e.g., weekly or aligned with the update cycle) cross-referenced against reported percent complete, direct conversations with site supervision before finalizing each update, and independent verification of progress on critical-path activities specifically, since those are the ones whose inaccuracy has the most consequence.
expertAnswer: Frames this as a broader competency and credibility risk for the planning function: a planning engineer who is purely a data-entry conduit for other people's numbers cannot meaningfully challenge or interpret those numbers, cannot add real value in progress meetings, and — if the numbers turn out to have been wrong or manipulated — bears professional exposure for having issued a report they never independently validated, which matters if that report is later relied upon in a dispute.
explanation: Processing status updates into P6 correctly is a scheduling skill; verifying those updates reflect real, achievable site conditions and that the logic still models actual construction intent is a planning skill — losing the second while retaining the first produces a mathematically clean but potentially fictional schedule.
reasoning: CPM calculation is only as trustworthy as its inputs. A planner who accepts every reported percent complete uncritically, and never revisits whether the network's logic still matches the real construction sequence, has reduced the planning function to data processing, forfeiting the judgment and verification that make the schedule a reliable management tool rather than merely an internally-consistent calculation.
commonMistakes: Believing a technically correct P6 update, on its own, is evidence the schedule is trustworthy.
Assuming foremen's self-reported percent complete requires no independent verification.
Not recognizing that logic can become outdated even if no one formally changes it, simply because site sequencing evolved without the schedule being revisited.
redFlags: Sees no problem with never visiting site or speaking to site engineers as part of the update cycle.
Cannot describe any verification step beyond data entry.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests professional accountability judgment beyond a simple 'not my fault' answer.

skill: Reconciling conflicting reporting requirements from multiple financially-interested stakeholders on a single project without compromising schedule integrity
scenario: A branded hotel renovation project has three stakeholders with different, partly conflicting scheduling needs: the hotel owner wants weekly updates focused on guest-room floor availability so they can plan phased reopening and revenue; the franchise brand's project office requires a rigid, standardized monthly report format tied to their global portfolio template, which does not naturally map to this project's phased-floor approach; and the project's lender requires quarterly milestone certification tied to specific disbursement-linked dates in the loan agreement, with any missed milestone triggering a formal notice process.
question: As the lead planning engineer, how would you structure the schedule and reporting process to serve all three stakeholders without creating contradictory information or missing a contractual/financial trigger?
expectedAnswer: Maintain one master schedule as the single source of truth, with a WBS/activity coding structure that captures floor-by-floor phasing explicitly (so guest-room floor availability can be reported natively) and that separately tags the lender's disbursement-linked milestones as their own identifiable, non-negotiable milestone set. From that one dataset, produce three distinct outputs: a weekly floor-availability view for the owner (a filtered layout grouped by floor/phase), a monthly report reformatted into the franchise brand's required template (a translation/mapping exercise from the master WBS into their fixed categories, not a separately maintained schedule), and a quarterly milestone certification report that explicitly tracks each lender-linked milestone's forecast versus required date, flagged well in advance of any risk of a miss so there is time to communicate before a formal notice is triggered. The critical discipline is that all three outputs are derived from the same underlying logic-linked dataset and data date, so they can never show contradictory dates.
strongAnswer: Notes that the lender's disbursement milestones should be given the highest monitoring priority and the longest early-warning lead time of the three, given the formal notice/default consequence of a miss, and recommends briefing the internal team on which specific milestones carry that financial trigger so they receive focused attention distinct from ordinary schedule management.
expertAnswer: Addresses the governance/political dimension: reconciling a franchise brand's rigid global template against a genuinely different phased-floor project structure often requires a documented crosswalk/mapping agreed with the brand's project office up front, rather than repeatedly renegotiating the mapping each reporting cycle; and recommends proactively flagging to the lender, well before any quarter-end, if a milestone is trending toward being missed, since surfacing that risk early (with a credible recovery plan) is materially better for the relationship and any contractual consequence than only reporting the miss after the fact in the formal certification.
explanation: Multiple financially-interested stakeholders each need a differently-shaped view of the same underlying scope; the solution is a single governed dataset with tailored, derived outputs — never separately maintained schedules — and a monitoring priority that reflects which stakeholder's requirement carries the most severe consequence if missed.
reasoning: As in any multi-stakeholder reporting situation, divergence between separately maintained views is the central risk; here it is compounded by real financial and contractual consequences (revenue phasing, brand compliance, loan default triggers) that make a reporting inconsistency far costlier than on an internal-only project, which raises both the technical requirement (one source of truth) and the professional judgment requirement (proactive early warning on the highest-consequence trigger).
commonMistakes: Building three separately maintained schedules or reports to match each stakeholder's format, risking drift and contradiction.
Treating all three stakeholders' requirements as equally weighted rather than recognizing the lender's milestone-linked consequence is the most severe.
Waiting until the formal quarterly certification to disclose a milestone at risk, rather than flagging it as soon as it becomes apparent.
redFlags: Cannot explain how to prevent the three outputs from contradicting each other over time.
No differentiated monitoring priority despite materially different consequences of a miss.
Would report a missed lender milestone only at the formal certification point with no earlier warning.

skill: Recognizing when a schedule has too little detail to support the contractor's own execution control, even though it satisfies the client's contractual reporting need
scenario: On a river bridge widening project, the client's contract only requires a Level 2 summary schedule of around 80 activities, tracking major milestones (falsework erection, deck pour per span, barrier/parapet works, surfacing, opening to traffic). The contractor's site team has been executing purely from this Level 2 schedule for four months, with no more detailed internal schedule, and is now struggling to coordinate falsework strike timing against deck curing requirements across five spans.
question: Before recommending a fix, what would you check first, and what does this situation reveal about level of detail?
expectedAnswer: Check whether a more detailed internal execution schedule was ever developed at all, or whether the team has genuinely been running site coordination purely off the 80-activity contractual summary schedule with no supporting detail underneath it. This situation illustrates that a schedule can be entirely adequate for one purpose (satisfying the client's contractual reporting requirement) while being genuinely inadequate for another (the contractor's own internal execution control) — the fix is not to add more detail to the client-facing Level 2 schedule, but to develop a separate, more granular internal control schedule (span-by-span falsework, pour, and curing sequencing with realistic curing durations and crane/formwork cycle logic) that the contractual summary schedule can continue to roll up from.
strongAnswer: Notes this is the reverse of the more commonly discussed level-of-detail problem (excessive detail overwhelming a schedule) — here the schedule is under-detailed relative to a genuine internal coordination need, and the appropriate fix mirrors the same principle: match the level of detail to the actual decisions that need to be supported, which differ for the client's contractual reporting purpose versus the contractor's own execution control purpose.
expertAnswer: Flags that this gap likely also has a resourcing/capability cause, not just a technical one — someone chose not to invest in developing an internal execution schedule, possibly because the Level 2 schedule was treated as 'the schedule' full stop rather than one of several tiers a competent planning function should maintain — and recommends this become a standing practice (an internal working schedule maintained regardless of what the contract itself requires) rather than a one-off fix limited to this bridge widening.
explanation: Level of detail should be judged against the specific decisions and audience it needs to serve; a schedule can simultaneously be exactly right for a contractual reporting purpose and badly wrong for a contractor's own internal execution control, and the fix is a second, purpose-built tier of detail, not a compromise edit to the first.
reasoning: The client's Level 2 requirement defines a contractual minimum, not a ceiling on what the contractor should internally maintain for its own coordination needs — treating the contractually mandated schedule as the only schedule the project needs conflates two different purposes that happen to share the same underlying scope.
commonMistakes: Assuming the contract's required level of detail defines everything the contractor needs internally.
Proposing to simply add more activities to the Level 2 client-facing schedule rather than building a separate internal control schedule.
Not recognizing this as a level-of-detail mismatch at all, and instead treating it purely as a falsework coordination problem.
redFlags: Cannot distinguish between the client's contractual reporting requirement and the contractor's own internal execution planning need.
Proposes cluttering the client-facing schedule with internal coordination detail it was never meant to carry.
p6Checks: Confirm whether a separate internal/working schedule exists in P6 (a different project or a more detailed WBS branch) beyond the 80-activity client submission.

Check whether falsework strike and deck curing durations are represented anywhere with real engineering-substantiated durations, or only implied by milestone-to-milestone gaps in the Level 2 schedule.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests judgment on transparency versus the risk of over-committing to detail the client did not ask for and might hold the contractor to.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding of maintaining a coherent multi-tier structure rather than two schedules drifting apart.

dimensions.guidance: Recommends a separate internal tier rather than compromising the client-facing schedule.

skill: Designing a multi-axis activity coding scheme that supports reporting by phase, terminal zone, and responsible party simultaneously without conflating them
scenario: A new airport terminal project involves a main contractor and 14 major subcontract packages (structure, facade, baggage handling system, MEP, fire life safety, IT/low-voltage, retail fit-out, etc.), spread across five terminal zones (piers A-D and the main check-in hall), with distinct handover phases (structural completion, MEP rough-in, fit-out, systems integration testing, operational readiness). The project controls manager wants monthly reports that can filter by any one of: responsible subcontractor, terminal zone, and handover phase, independently.
question: Design the Activity ID and Activity Code structure you would use, and explain how you decided what goes into the ID versus what becomes a code.
expectedAnswer: Terminal Zone is a good candidate for the WBS and/or Activity ID, since every activity belongs to exactly one zone and zone is a stable, hierarchical, natural grouping for the whole life of the project (e.g., an ID pattern like PIERB-STR-0120 for Pier B, Structural discipline, sequence 0120). Responsible Subcontractor and Handover Phase should be dedicated Activity Codes rather than baked into the ID: a subcontractor can work across multiple zones and phases, and a given activity's phase classification is a status-like attribute that could be reassigned or refined as the project matures (e.g., a phase boundary redefinition) — encoding either into a fixed ID would break as soon as those cross-cutting realities appear. The result is a WBS/ID structure organized by Zone (and discipline), with 'Responsible Subcontractor' and 'Handover Phase' as two separate, independently filterable Activity Code fields, letting the project controls manager slice the same 3,000+ activity dataset by any one dimension without restructuring anything.
strongAnswer: Notes that Discipline could arguably sit in either the ID (as here) or as a code, and explains the deciding factor: if discipline reporting is needed independently of zone (e.g., 'show me all MEP activities across every zone'), a code handles that more cleanly than an ID prefix that ties discipline to a specific zone segment; recommends testing the design against the actual reporting questions the team will ask, not just today's known three dimensions.
expertAnswer: Highlights that Handover Phase in particular should be modeled carefully, since 'phase' can mean either a genuinely sequential state each activity passes through (better suited to a status-like Activity Code that gets updated) or a hard scope boundary (better suited to WBS or a separate sub-project) — conflating the two is a common design error; recommends the coding standard be documented in a formal coding dictionary approved at project set-up and circulated to all 14 subcontractors so their own reporting/interfaces align with the main contractor's structure from day one, rather than reconciling mismatched coding after the fact.
explanation: Good coding design places stable, single-valued, hierarchical attributes (here, Zone) into the WBS/Activity ID, and places cross-cutting or potentially-reassignable attributes (Subcontractor, Handover Phase) into independently filterable Activity Codes, so that any one of the three reporting dimensions can be sliced without restructuring the dataset.
reasoning: An Activity ID or WBS position encodes one fixed hierarchy; forcing more than one independent reporting dimension into that same fixed hierarchy either breaks down (an activity cannot have two 'positions' at once) or requires arbitrary compromises about which dimension takes precedence — Activity Codes exist to add additional, independent, filterable dimensions without that constraint.
commonMistakes: Trying to encode all three dimensions (zone, subcontractor, phase) into a single rigid Activity ID string.
Using Activity Codes for everything, abandoning any logical structure in the ID itself.
Not distinguishing a genuinely sequential status attribute (phase) from a fixed scope attribute when deciding where it belongs.
redFlags: Proposes an ID scheme that cannot represent a subcontractor working across multiple zones.
Cannot explain the difference between a stable hierarchical attribute and a cross-cutting reportable attribute.
p6Checks: Activity Codes dictionary — confirm distinct, project-level (not just global) codes exist for Responsible Subcontractor and Handover Phase.
WBS/EPS structure — confirm Terminal Zone forms a clean hierarchical branch that the Gantt and reports can roll up by.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If the client later asks for reporting by a fourth dimension — say, systems integration test package — how would your structure accommodate that without rework?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the design is genuinely extensible.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Should Activity Codes be defined at the Global (enterprise) level or the Project level in P6 for a program like this, and why might that matter?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests awareness of P6's global vs project-level code scope and its implications for a multi-project airport program.

dimensions.guidance: Correctly separates ID/WBS-suitable attributes from Activity-Code-suitable attributes.

dimensions.name: reasoning
dimensions.guidance: Explains the decision logic (stable/hierarchical vs cross-cutting/reassignable), not just states a scheme.

dimensions.name: practicalApplication
dimensions.guidance: Gives a concrete, realistic ID pattern and code scheme for the airport terminal.

skill: Diagnosing organizational/cultural reasons a technically sound schedule is not actually used to run the project
scenario: On a mountain road tunnel project, the planning department produces a technically excellent, fully logic-linked, well-maintained P6 schedule every week. However, the site agent and tunnel superintendent openly run the actual excavation and lining operations from a whiteboard in the site office and their own experience, rarely referring to the P6 schedule at all, and treat the weekly planning report as something they sign off on without really reading.
question: What is most likely going wrong here, given that the schedule itself is technically sound? What would you investigate, and how would you address it?
explanation: A technically excellent schedule that is not actually used to run the project most often indicates a disconnect between the planning function and site operations rather than a technical schedule defect — common root causes include: the schedule was built without real site-team involvement, so it does not reflect how the site agent and superintendent actually think about and sequence tunneling operations (e.g., it may not be organized by excavation ring/chainage in a way that matches how they track advance); the schedule's update cadence (weekly) is too slow for the day-to-day, near-real-time decisions tunneling operations actually require, which the whiteboard fills instead; or a trust/credibility gap exists because the schedule has been wrong or unresponsive to real site conditions before, and the site team has learned not to rely on it. The investigation should include direct conversation with the site agent and superintendent about how they actually plan their week, comparison of the P6 structure against the whiteboard's structure and logic, and a review of whether the schedule's historical forecasts have actually tracked real outcomes.
reasoning: A schedule's value depends entirely on whether the people executing the work actually use it to make decisions; technical correctness (valid logic, accurate float, clean CPM math) is necessary but not sufficient for that — if the tool does not match the operational rhythm, granularity, or trusted track record the site team needs, they will build and use a parallel informal system instead, and the 'official' schedule becomes a reporting artifact disconnected from real execution, which is itself a serious planning failure even though no CPM rule was broken.
commonMistakes: Assuming the schedule is fine simply because it is technically correct, and blaming the site team for not using it.
Not investigating whether the schedule's structure and cadence actually match how tunneling operations are really managed day to day.
Treating this as a training/compliance problem to be solved by insisting people use P6, without addressing why they stopped trusting or needing it.
redFlags: Sees no problem as long as the schedule itself is technically defensible, regardless of whether site actually uses it.
Proposes only a compliance fix ('make them use it') with no investigation into the underlying disconnect.
p6Checks: Compare the P6 activity breakdown and update granularity against how the whiteboard organizes daily tunneling advance (by ring/chainage, shift, or face).
Review recent weekly forecasts against actual outcomes to check whether the schedule has a credible track record of accuracy from the site team's perspective.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If you find the schedule's weekly cadence is simply too slow for tunneling decision-making, what would you propose instead, without abandoning the CPM baseline entirely?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate can propose a workable near-real-time supplementary tool (e.g., a daily advance log feeding into the weekly P6 update) rather than an all-or-nothing fix.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What risk does this disconnect create if a delay claim or dispute arises later?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests awareness that a schedule the site team demonstrably never used undermines its credibility as a contemporaneous record in any later dispute.

dimensions.name: reasoning
dimensions.guidance: Identifies multiple plausible organizational/cultural causes, not just one.

dimensions.name: professionalJudgment
dimensions.guidance: Recognizes technical correctness alone does not guarantee real operational use.

dimensions.name: practicalApplication
dimensions.guidance: Proposes a concrete investigation and remediation path involving the site team.

skill: Recognizing when a WBS is technically complete and hierarchical but still practically unworkable because sibling elements are not mutually exclusive
scenario: A municipal water treatment plant project's WBS includes, at the same level under 'Process Systems': 'Filtration System', 'Chemical Dosing System', and 'Electrical & Instrumentation'. During execution, the team finds that dosing pump control panels and cabling — clearly electrical/instrumentation scope — have been coded inconsistently by different engineers, sometimes under 'Chemical Dosing System' and sometimes under 'Electrical & Instrumentation', because both WBS elements plausibly seem to own that scope.
question: Is this a valid WBS despite representing all the scope somewhere? What principle is at risk here, and how would you fix it going forward?
expectedAnswer: The WBS may satisfy the 100% rule (all scope appears somewhere) but is failing the mutual-exclusivity principle: sibling WBS elements should have clear, non-overlapping boundaries so that any given piece of scope has exactly one correct home. Here, control panels and cabling for the dosing system plausibly belong to either 'Chemical Dosing System' (functionally) or 'Electrical & Instrumentation' (technically/by discipline), and without an explicit boundary rule, different engineers will code it inconsistently — which corrupts cost/progress reporting by system, because dosing system cost and progress will be understated wherever E&I scope was coded elsewhere, and vice versa. The fix is to define and document an explicit boundary rule (e.g., 'all control panels, instrumentation and cabling are coded under Electrical & Instrumentation regardless of which process system they serve, with a cross-reference/code so dosing-related E&I scope can still be reported by system if needed') and to apply it retroactively to reconcile already-miscoded activities.
strongAnswer: Notes that this is a very common WBS design tension between organizing by process system versus by discipline, and that the fix does not have to eliminate one axis — a documented boundary rule for the primary WBS hierarchy, combined with a secondary Activity Code for the other axis (e.g., keep E&I as the WBS home, but tag dosing-related E&I activities with a 'Process System = Chemical Dosing' code), preserves both reporting views without ambiguity about primary ownership.
expertAnswer: Points out the downstream cost-control consequence: if cost accounts are tied to WBS elements (common in EPC-style project controls), inconsistent coding directly corrupts earned value and cost-to-complete reporting by system, which can mislead the process engineering team about which system is actually over or under budget — recommends this kind of boundary ambiguity be caught and resolved during WBS design review, before baseline, by walking through several deliberately ambiguous scope examples with the whole team rather than assuming the hierarchy is self-explanatory.
explanation: A WBS can technically cover 100% of scope and still fail as a usable structure if sibling elements are not mutually exclusive — ambiguous boundaries between plausible homes for the same scope produce inconsistent coding, which corrupts any reporting built on the WBS.
reasoning: WBS decomposition requires two properties together: completeness (100% of scope represented) and mutual exclusivity (each piece of scope belongs to exactly one element). Completeness alone, without a clear boundary rule between elements whose scope plausibly overlaps, still produces an unreliable structure because different people will make different, inconsistent judgment calls about where ambiguous scope belongs.
commonMistakes: Concluding the WBS is fine because everything is represented somewhere, without checking whether boundaries are unambiguous.
Not recognizing process-system-vs-discipline as a common source of WBS boundary ambiguity.
Proposing to just 'communicate better' rather than documenting an explicit, checkable boundary rule.
redFlags: Cannot identify mutual exclusivity as a distinct WBS principle from completeness.
Has no concrete mechanism to resolve or prevent ongoing miscoding.
p6Checks: Cost Accounts / WBS assignment — audit a sample of E&I-type activities across all process systems to check for coding consistency against the documented boundary rule.
WBS dictionary — confirm a written scope-boundary definition exists for each element, not just element names.

followUpQuestions.prompt: How would you reconcile activities that were already miscoded before the boundary rule was documented, without disrupting reported cost/progress history?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests practical judgment on retroactive correction versus accepting some historical inconsistency.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Is there a case where a dual-axis reporting need like this is better solved by changing the primary WBS axis entirely, rather than adding a boundary rule plus a code?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests deeper WBS design judgment about choosing the right primary axis versus patching a secondary one.

dimensions.name: reasoning
dimensions.guidance: Explains how ambiguous boundaries corrupt cost/progress reporting by system.

dimensions.name: practicalApplication

skill: Recognizing insufficient information to choose a schedule development approach and identifying what governance decision must precede that choice
scenario: A contractor has been awarded an offshore wind turbine repowering contract: decommissioning 40 aging turbines and installing 25 larger-capacity replacement turbines on the same foundations at an operating wind farm, while 60 other turbines at the same site continue generating power and must not be taken offline. The planning director asks the lead planning engineer to 'get the execution schedule built' within two weeks.
question: Before committing to a schedule development approach and structure, what critical information is missing, and why would proceeding without it risk building the wrong kind of schedule entirely?
expectedAnswer: Several critical pieces of information are missing that would each materially change the right development approach: (1) the operational constraint regime — what access windows, safety exclusion zones, and grid-connection sequencing rules apply around the 60 turbines that must stay live, since this could make the project resource/logistics-constrained (limited vessel and crew windows) rather than purely CPM-logic-driven; (2) whether decommissioning and installation proceed turbine-by-turbine in a fixed sequence or can be parallelized across multiple vessel spreads, which determines whether this is closer to a repetitive/linear operation or a genuinely parallel multi-path CPM project; (3) weather/marine-window seasonality, which for offshore work is often the dominant schedule driver and needs to be built into calendars and risk contingency from the start, not retrofitted later; and (4) whether the wind farm operator (a third party, not the client directly) has independent approval authority over outage windows, which is a stakeholder/governance question, not just a technical one. Committing to a schedule structure and approach within two weeks without first pinning these down risks building a conventional CPM-logic schedule that looks complete but misses the actual real-world constraint (vessel/weather-window availability and third-party outage approval) that will really govern the project's achievable pace.
strongAnswer: Frames the immediate need as a scoping/basis-of-schedule exercise, not schedule-building itself: recommends the two-week period be used to nail down the operational constraint regime and marine-window data with input from marine operations and the wind farm operator, and to explicitly agree with the planning director that a credible schedule cannot be produced in two weeks without that information — proposing instead a phased approach (a preliminary Level 1 schedule immediately, with the fully developed execution schedule following once constraints are confirmed).
expertAnswer: Recognizes this scenario sits at the intersection of several related concepts — resource/production-rate-driven scheduling for repetitive marine operations, rolling-wave development given evolving design/logistics maturity, and stakeholder governance with a non-client third party — and that senior-level judgment here means knowing which single piece of missing information is most likely to be the actual project bottleneck (very plausibly the vessel/weather window and third-party outage approval process, not CPM logic at all) and prioritizing getting that confirmed first, rather than spending the two weeks building network logic that will need to be substantially reworked once the real constraint is understood.
explanation: This scenario deliberately withholds information that would change the fundamental schedule development approach, testing whether a senior candidate recognizes that 'build the schedule' is premature without first resolving operational-constraint, sequencing, seasonal, and third-party-governance questions that determine what kind of schedule this actually needs to be.
reasoning: Different underlying project realities call for fundamentally different schedule development approaches (parallel multi-path CPM versus resource/production-rate-driven linear scheduling versus vessel/window-constrained sequencing), and choosing the wrong one before confirming the true operational driver produces a schedule that looks complete but does not represent the project's real constraint, which is far more damaging on a technically and operationally complex marine project than on a conventional building project.
commonMistakes: Starting to build detailed CPM logic immediately without first confirming the true operational constraint regime.
Treating this as a purely technical scheduling problem and missing the third-party (wind farm operator) governance dimension.
Assuming a two-week timeline is simply tight but achievable without pushing back on what is realistically possible without more information.
redFlags: Commits to a full execution schedule and structure within two weeks without first flagging the missing operational and governance information.
Cannot articulate why marine/weather windows might be the dominant schedule driver rather than CPM logic.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests stakeholder-management skill in pushing back constructively on a leadership request.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If it turns out vessel availability is the dominant constraint, how would that change the schedule's structure compared to a conventional activity-by-activity CPM network?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate can connect the missing-information diagnosis back to a concrete change in development approach.

skill: Performing a forward pass through a short chain of activities that mixes Finish-to-Start and Start-to-Start relationships
scenario: A cross-country gas pipeline section has three activities under a day-1 start convention (first activity Early Start = Day 1): 'Trenching' (Duration 10 days, starts Day 1), 'Pipe Stringing & Welding' (Duration 8 days), linked to Trenching by a Start-to-Start relationship with a 3-day lag (the welding crew can begin 3 days after trenching starts, once enough trench is open), and 'Backfill & Reinstatement' (Duration 6 days), linked to Pipe Stringing & Welding by a Finish-to-Start relationship with zero lag.
question: Using the day-1 start convention, calculate the Early Finish of 'Backfill & Reinstatement'.

options.label: A
options.text: Day 16

options.label: B
options.text: Day 17

options.label: C
options.text: Day 18

options.label: D
options.text: Day 24

explanation: Trenching: ES=1, EF=1+10-1=10. Pipe Stringing & Welding (SS +3 days from Trenching's start): ES=1+3=4, EF=4+8-1=11. Backfill & Reinstatement (FS, zero lag from Welding's finish): ES=11+1=12, EF=12+6-1=17. Early Finish of Backfill & Reinstatement = Day 17.
reasoning: The SS relationship ties Welding's start to Trenching's start plus the 3-day lag, not to Trenching's finish — this is what allows the two crews to overlap and is what makes the pipeline sequence faster than a fully sequential (FS) chain would be. The subsequent FS relationship into Backfill then behaves normally, waiting for Welding's full finish plus the day-1-convention handover.
commonMistakes: Treating the Trenching-to-Welding relationship as Finish-to-Start instead of Start-to-Start with lag, ignoring the 3-day overlap entirely and landing on Day 24.
Applying the Backfill relationship as if it started directly on Welding's Early Finish day without the +1 day-1-convention handover, landing on Day 16.
Forgetting to subtract 1 when converting Early Start plus Duration into Early Finish under the day-1 convention, landing on Day 18.
redFlags: Cannot correctly apply a Start-to-Start relationship with lag in a forward-pass calculation.
Confuses SS and FS relationship mechanics.
p6Checks: Activities view — Relationships tab to confirm the Trenching-to-Welding relationship is genuinely SS with a 3-day lag, not FS.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If the SS lag were increased to 6 days instead of 3, what would the new Early Finish of Backfill & Reinstatement be, and why does the answer not simply shift by 3 days in every case?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate can recompute and recognize when a changed lag becomes the new critical driver versus when it is absorbed elsewhere.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Walk through each activity's Early Start and Early Finish one at a time, paying close attention to which relationship type governs each handover.
followUpQuestions.purpose: Diagnoses where the SS-versus-FS mechanics break down for the candidate.
